Intro of PM

Introduction to Project Management (University of Sydney) 

Section 1

What is Project management?

• “A temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result” – PMBOK Guide.

• “The application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities to meet the project requirements” – PMBOK Guide.

6 constraints of project management

• Scope (size).

• Cost. 

• Resources. 

• Quality.

• Schedule.

• Risks. 

Project life cycle

• Predictable stages of all projects.

• Life cycles allow for control to assure that the project is proceeding correctly and the results will satisfy the customer. 

Project life cycle stages

• Selecting and initiating.

• Planning.

• Executing.

• Closing and realising.

Project management body of knowledge (PMBOK) – PMBOK process groups

• Initiating.

• Planning.

• Executing.

• Monitoring and controlling.

• Closing.

PMBOK knowledge areas

• Integration management.

• Scope management.

• Time management.

• Cost management.

• Quality management.

• Human resources management.

• Risk management.

• Procurement management.

• Stakeholder management.

Selecting and prioritising projects

• Consider the potential and success of each project.

• Are the demands/resources enough?

• Do you have the support?

Project success

• Meeting agreements.

• Customer success/satisfaction.

• Performing organisations success.

• Project teams’ success.

Reasons for failure

• Not enough resources available.

• Not enough time given to complete project.

• Expectations of project are unclear.

• Not all parties agree on terms.

• Stakeholders disagree on the expectations of the project.

• Adequate project planning is not used.

Types of projects

• Classifying by industry.

• Classifying by size.

• Classifying by timing of project scope identify.

• Classifying by application.

Strategic Planning process

• step 1: Strategy Attributes Definition

• step 2: Strategic Priorities Formulation

• step 3: Strategy Description

• step 4: Strategy Cascading

• step 5: Strategy Execution

Strategic analysis

• SWOT analysis:

◦ Strengths.

◦ Weaknesses.

◦ Opportunities.

◦ Threats.

• Analysis of internal and external environments.

Porters five forces model of competition – firm and industry level thinking

• Threats of new entrants.

• Determinants of buyer power.

• Threat of substitute products.

• Determinants of supplier power.

• Rivalry among existing firms.

Guiding principles – Vision and mission

• The vision describes the organisation of the future.

• The mission statement provides a mechanism for achieving the vision.

Mission statement considerations

• Purpose.

• Beliefs.

• Core values.

• Culture.

• Primary business areas.

• Primary customers.

Strategic objectives

• Means of achieving the vision and mission.

• Short and long term goals.

• Effective objectives are SMART:

◦ Specific.

◦ Measurable.

◦ Achievable.

◦ Results-based.

◦ Time-specific.

Portfolio Alignment

• Assesses the organisation’s ability to perform.

• Portfolio.

• Programs.

• Projects and subprojects.

Flow-down objectives

• How to implement strategic objects.

• Objectives may be implemented through ongoing operations.

• Example: Promote the university internationally and through promotions through open days and new scholarships etc.

Portfolio

• “A collection of projects or programs and other work that are grouped together to facilitate effective management of that work to meet strategic business objectives” – PMBOK Guide.

• There should be a sense of balance with portfolios between different sized projects and comparing their risks and schedule.

Programs

• Programs are “related projects”.

• Specific projects within a program are of limited time.

Projects and subprojects

• “A smaller portion of the overall project created when a project is subdivided into more manageable components” – PMBOK Guide.

Identifying potential projects

• Statement of work:

◦ Narrative description of products of services to be provided by the project” – PMBOK Guide.

• Business case:

◦ Provides the information needed from a business standpoint to determine if the project is worth the investment” – PMBOK Guide.

The business case

• Introduction.

• Background.

• Project objective.

• Critical assumption and constraints.

• Options, analysis and recommendation.

• Project requirements.

• Budget.

• Schedule.

• Cost.

Methods for selecting projects

• Ensure overall organisational priorities are understood, agreed upon and communicated.

• Think to yourself, which project offers better profit, more success and is in high demand with enough resources.

• Include financial and scoring models.

• Three different approaches include:

◦ Use financial analysis as the primary means of determining which projects are selected.

◦  Use financial models as screening devices to qualify projects for a scoring model.

◦ Financial justification is one factor in a multi-factor scoring model.

Net Present Value (NPV) Analysis

• NPV analysis is a method of calculating the expected net monetary gain or loss from a project by discounting all expected future cash inflows and outflows to the present point in time.

•

◦ Worth of $1 in n years’ time is lesser than $1 today.

◦ NPV accounts for the time value of money.

• Higher the NPV, the better.

• The find the value of $1 in n years we use:

◦ A=P(1+r)^2（r mean rate）

• NPV is therefore the present worth of $1 in n years:

◦ P=A/(1+r)^2

Benefit-cost ratio model

• Divide the cash flow by the initial cash outlay.
BCR = Present Value of Costs / Present Value of Benefits

• A ratio above 1.0 means the project is expected to profit.

Return on investment (ROI)

• ROI is calculated by subtracting the project costs from the benefits and then dividing by the costs.
ROI = (Benefits - Costs) / Costs*100%

• The higher the ROI, the better.

• Many organisations have a required rate of return or minimum acceptable rate of return on investment for projects.

Internal Rate of Return (IRR) model

• It is simply the interest rate that you are earning on your investment when you consider the stream of payments or benefits you expect to receive.

◦ Calculate the percentage return expected on the project investment.

◦ A ratio above the current cost of capital is considered positive. 

◦ IRR can be calculated by finding the discount rate that makes NPV equal to 0.（IRR is r (rate) in NPV）

• To calculate IRR, we need to ask what is the interest rate that will convert the stream of payments into a present value that equals the amount being invested (or spent)?

Using financial model to select projects

• The payback period is calculated by how many years it would require to pay back the initial project investment.

• Shorter payback periods are desirable.

• Financial models ensure that projects make sense from a cost and return perspective.

Using a scoring model to select projects

• Develop a list of project selection criteria.

• Does the project suit the organisations objectives?

• Is there going to be profit?

• Do we have enough resources?

Using a scoring model (matrix) to select projects

• Identifying potential criteria.

• Determine mandatory criteria.

• Weighting criteria.

• Transparency.

Evaluating projects based on criterion

• Evaluate one criterion at a time.

• Rate each project on the particular criterion.

• Multiplying the rating by the weight assignment to the criteria.

• Select the highest scoring project(s).

Other considerations in prioritising projects

• Which project will be started first.

• The urgency of each project.

• The cost delaying the expected benefits from various projects.

• Practical details concerning time.

• Project termination.

Negotiate to secure the project

• Negotiate the amount of money to be paid for a project.

• Negotiate contractual terms, schedule, specific personnel, quality standards and reporting mechanisms.

• A project manager attempts to find a solution to secure project work with enough project potential.

Section 3

Organisational structure

• Consists of work assignments, reporting, relationships and decision making responsibility.

◦ Functional organisations.

◦ Projectised organisations.

◦ Matrix organisations.

Functional organisation

• A hierarchical organisation where each employee has one clear superior, the staff are grouped by areas of specialisation  and managed by a person with expertise in the area” – PMBOK Guide.

• Functional manager controls the budget, makes project decisions and coordinates project communications.

 Projectised organisation

• "Any organisational structure in which the project manager has full authority to assign projects, apply resources and direct work to personnel assigned to the project" - PMBOK Guide.

• The project manager has autho irty for budgets, personnel and decision making.

Matrix organisation

• “Any organisational structure in which the project manager shares responsibilities with the functional managers for assigning priorities and directing work of persons assigned to the project” – PMBOK Guide.

• The project manager and functional manager share authority over budgets, personnel, and decision making.

Organisational structures comparison

none

Functional

Matrix

Advantages

- Good discipline
- specific knowledge
- Easy fro central control
- Effective for shared resources
- One “boos”
- Clear career path for professionals

- Flexible 
- Easy to share resources
- Good cooperation between departments
- More input for decisions
- Wide acceptance of decisions
- Good discipline-specific knowledge 
- Effective integration on project
- Increased knowledge transfer between projects 

- Break down department barriers
- Shorter response time
- Quicker decisions
- One “boss” 
- Enhanced project team identity
- Customer focus
- Effective integration on project 

Disadvantages

- Slow communication between departments 
- Slow response to change 
- Slow decision making

- Two “bosses”
 Many sources of conflict
- More meetings
- Slow reaction time
- Hard to monitor and control

- Duplication of resources
Rules not always respected
- Potential lessons learned can be lost
- Discipline-specific knowledge an slip
- Less career continuity for project team members 

360-degree performance reviews

• The functional manager seeks feedback from a representative sample of the staff that have worked with that project team member to provide feedback on a 360-degree form.

Organisational culture and its impact on projects

• Motivate the ethical actions and communications of managers and subordinates.

• Determine how people are treated, controlled and rewarded.

• Establish how cooperation, competition, conflict and decision making are handled and encourage personal commitment to the organisation and justification for its behaviour.

Successful organisation culture characteristics

• Support for the cross-functional teams.

• Stakeholder involvement.

• Integrity

• Innovation

• Open communication.

• Respect for individuals.

Project manager behaviours

• Responsible.

• Respectful.

• Fairness.

• Honest.

Section 4

General Project life cycle

• Selecting & Initiating Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Charter.

• Planning Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Kick-off.

• Executing Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Project result.

• Closing & Realizing Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Administrative closure.

Define-measure-analyse-improve-control (DMAIC) model

• Selecting & Initiating Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Charter.

• Planning Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Kick-off.

• Executing Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Project result.

• Closing & Realising Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Administrative closure.

Research and development (R&D) project life cycle model

• Define Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Problem statement.

• Measure Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Fact gathering defined and facts collected.

• Analyze Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Root causes identified and statistically proven.

• Improve Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Solution implemented.

• Control Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Methods in place to maintain improvements.

Construction project life cycle

• Idea Generation Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Opportunity Analysis.

• Idea Screening Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Business Case.

• Concept Development Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Proven Concept.

• Validation Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Prototype.

• Transition Phase: Approval to proceed granted via First lot and hand-off.

Information systems (IS) project life cycle

• Pre-planning Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Scope definition and execution strategy.

• Design Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Procurement and construction documents.

• Procurement Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Materials and s2ervices.

• Construction Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Facilities and processes.

• Start up Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Production attainment.

Agile project life cycle

• Concept Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Charter.

• Requirements gathering Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Detailed requirements.

• Design Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Systems and detailed designs.

• Code Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Code.

• Test Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Unit and system tests.

• Turnover Phase: Approval to proceed granted via Training and documentation

Section 5

Scope panning process

• Collect project requirements.

• Define project’s scope.

• Create a work breakdown structure.

Scope planning

• Total scope = product scope + project scope.

• Product scope- “the features and functions that characterise a product, service or result” – PMBOK Guide.

• Project scope – “The work that must be performed to deliver a product, service or result” – PMBOK Guide.

Collecting requirements

• Make sure project objectives are clear to the team.

• Gather stakeholders input.

• Use voice of the customer techniques (VOC).

• Seek a high-level description.

Requirements matrix

• Traceable.

• Clear.

• Measurable.

• Prioritised.

Scope definition

• “The processes of developing a detailed description of the project and product” – PMBOK Guide.

• Conforms to project charter and project objectives.

• States deliverables, constraints and assumptions.

• Establishes boundaries of work.

Scope creep

• Scope creep occurs:

◦ When components of work or activity have poorly defined entry and exit criteria’s.

◦ When customers ask for additional features of products or services to be added.

How to define scope

Determine objectives.

List deliverables.

Gather stakeholder input.

Define scope for each deliverable

Defining scope boundaries.

Create scope statement.

Work breakdown structure (WBS)

• A tool used to progressively divide project work into smaller pieces.

• Identify deliverables.

• A framework used as a basis for further planning, execution and control.

Why use a WBS?

• Adds discipline and visibility to project planning,

• Basics for planning schedules, resources, cost, quality and risk.

• Useful in determining where and why problems occur.

• Helpful in project communications.

• Used as a template for future project planning.

WBS format

• Indented outline: Hierarchical text structure using indentation levels to show main points and subpoints.

• Organisational chart: Visual diagram of a company’s structure, showing roles and reporting lines.

• Free format: Unstructured layout with no predefined organization or formatting rules.

 WBS elements/components and dictionary

• WBS component/element – “an entry in the WBS that can be at any level” – PMBOK Guide.

• WBS dictionary – “a document that describes each component in the WBS … includes a brief description, defined deliverable(s), a lost if associated activities and sometimes other information” – PMBOK Guide.

Work Packages

• ”A deliverable … at the lowest level of each branch of a WBS” – PMBOK Guide.

• Work activities are defined and makes no sense to break further down.

WBS by phase

• Groups deliverables byproject stages (e.g., design → build → test).  

WBS by design/product components

•  Structures deliverables by physical parts (e.g., engine, chassis for a car). 

WBS by work function 

• WBS by work function: Organizes tasks byspecialized roles (e.g., engineering, marketing).

WBS structure considerations

• Have 3-9 child elements for each parent.

• Uniquely name each component in the WBS.

Establish change control

• Plans must be made for dealing with change.

• Every change to a project must be formally proposed, example, using a form.

• Change request – “request to expand or reduce the project scope, modify policies, processes, plans or procedures, modify costs or budgets, or revise schedules” – PMBOK Guide.

• Change control system – “a collection of formally documented procedures that define how project deliverables and documentation will be controlled, changed and approved” – PMBOK Guide.

Activities

• “A component of work performed during the course of a project” – PMBOK Guide.

Section 6

Project time management processes

Define activities.

Sequence activities.

Estimate activity resources.

Develop schedule.

Control schedule.

Program Evaluation and review technique (PERT)

• Estimates most likely time needed to complete a project.

• Estimates level of confidence in completing a project in a particular time.

• Useful in research and development projects.

Critical path method (CPM)

• Used in very large projects.

• Minimum total project duration.

• Useful in the construction industry.

Activity on Node (AON) pr Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM)

• Work activities are represented by a node and arrows connect activities representing the work of the event.

• Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM) - "a schedule network diagramming technique in which the scheduled activities are represented by boxes or nodes…" - PMBOK Guide.

Creation of Project Schedules

• Identify all activities.

• Determine logical order in network diagram.

• Assign resources to each activity.

• Estimate time required for that activity.

• Compare emerging schedule with imposed dates.

• Consider project budget and cash flow, quality demands and risk factors.

The project managers’ responsibility

• Resist pressure to dictate a schedule.

• Determine a schedule that is possible.

• Persuade stakeholders that the schedule makes sense.

• Deliver the project per the agreed-upon schedule.

List project milestones

• Complete toon of a major deliverables.

• Completion of a critical activity.

• Prior to a large financial commitment.

• Merging point in the project schedule.

Sequence activities

• Predecessor activity - "the scheduled activity that determines when the logical successor activity can begin or end" - PMBOK Guide.

• The following activity is called a successor activity.

• Place a successor activity after its predecessor.

• Successor activity - "The schedule activity that follows a predecessor activity, as determined by their logical relationship" - PMBOK Guide.

Leads and lags

• The most common type of logical dependency is Finish-to-start (FS).

• Leads are helpful if a project needs to be completed quickly.

• Finish-to-start -"the logical relationship where initiation of work of the successor activity depends on completion of work of the predecessor activity." - PMBOK Guide.

• Lead - "a modification of a logical relationship that allows an acceleration of the successor activity." - PMBOK Guide.

• Lag - "a modification of a logical relationship that directs a delay in the successor activity" - PMBOK Guide.

Finish-to-Finish Relationships

• Finish-to-finish- "the logical relationship where completion of work of the successor activity cannot finish until the completion of work of the predecessor activity" - PMBOK Guide.

Start-to-start relationships

• Start-to-start - "The logical relationship where initiation of the successor schedule activity depends on the initiation of the predecessor schedule activity" - PMBOK Guide.

Start-to-finish relationships

 • Start-to-finish - "the logical relationship where completion of the successor schedule activity is dependent on the initiation of the predecessor schedule activity" - PMBOK Guide.

Activity Duration Estimation

• Changing assumptions and constraints could change estimates.

• Duration - "The total number of work periods (not including holidays or other non-work time) required to complete a schedule activity." PMBOK Guide.

Estimate activity duration

• Identify the output that will be created.

• Identify the skill level required to perform the work.

• Disregard predetermined completion points.

• When using a past project as a guide, use actual time not initial

Estimates for activities.

• Keep time estimates in the same unit of measure.

• Elapsed units versus normal units (eg. Days versus days, or melon versus months).

Suggestions for creating realistic time estimates

Verify all time estimations with the people doing the work.

Estimate times of completion of work without initial reference to a calendar.

Make sure all time units are identical: working days, work week, months (consider time off for company holidays).

Consider time constraints - unexpected meetings, interruptions, inaccuracy in work instructions, emergencies/illness, learning curves, vacation, rework, resources pr information not available on time.

Acknowledge tendency toward optimistic or pessimistic estimations.

First establish a realistic estimate.

Adjust estimates based on size, familiarity, and complexity differences.

Learning Curves

• The more times a person performs an activating, the better and faster he or she becomes.

• Rate of improvement can be studied and predicted.

• Time necessary to perform an activity is calculated based upon a rate of improvement.

• Time estimates are found in learning curve tables.

• Rapid learning leads to faster performances times.

• PMs should plan for learning that takes place.

• PMs should create and sustain an environment that encourages and expects rapid learning.

Develop Project Schedules

• Identify the critical path:

◦ Two-ass method and enumeration method.

◦ Critical path - “…the sequence of activities that determines the duration of the project…the longest path through the project.” PMBOK Guide.

Two-Pass Method

• Used to determine the amount of slack each activity has.

• Make two logical passes through the constructed network:

◦ The forward pass.

◦ The backward pass.

• Forward pass - “the calculation of the early start and early finish dates for the uncompleted portions of all network activities.” PMBOK Guide.

Times important to each activity

• Early start date (EF) - “the earliest possible point in time on which uncompleted portions of a schedule activity can start…” PMBOK Guide.

• Early finish date (ES) - “the earliest possible point in time on which uncompleted portions of a schedule activity can finish…” PMBOK Guide.

• Late start date (EF) - “the latest possible point in time that a schedule activity may begin…” PMBOK Guide.

• Late finish date (ES) - “the latest possible point in time that a schedule activity may be completed…” PMBOK Guide.

Schedule example first pass

• Start at the beginning of the project and ask how soon each activity can begin and end. 

Second or Backward Pass

• How late can each activity be finished and started?

• Backward pass - “the calculation of late finish dates and late start dates for the uncompleted portions of all schedule activities.” PMBOK Guide.

Schedule example second pass

• Start at the end of the project and ask how late each activity can finish and begin.

Float and the critical path

• Compute the critical path based on float (slack).

• Activities with no float or very little float need to be scheduled very carefully.

• Float = Late Start – Early Start (Float = LS – ES).

• Critical path is the sequence of activities that have no float.

• Total float - “the total amount of time a schedule activity may be delayed from its early start date without delaying the project finish date.” PMBOK Guide.

• Free float - “the amount of time a schedule activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any immediately following schedule activities” PMBOK Guide.

 Enumeration Method

• All paths are identified and timed if the team needs to compress the schedule.

Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT)

•  Aid to understanding how variability in the duration of individual activities impacts the entire project schedule.

• Create 3 estimates of time to complete each activity:

◦ Optimistic.

◦ Most likely.

◦ Pessimistic.

• Estimated time = [Optimistic +4(Most likely) + Pessimistic]/6

• PERT considerations

• Advantages:

◦ Reinforces the degree of uncertainty that exists in project schedules.-Calculations indicate that expected time is longer than most likely time.

• Difficulties:

◦ Takes more effort to create 3 estimates.

◦ No guarantee how good the estimates are.

◦ May underestimate the risk of a schedule running long.

Show the project schedule on a Gantt Chart

• An easier to understand tool for communicating a project schedule.

• A horizontal bar chart showing each activity early start and finish.

• Show a bar for each activity stretched over a time line.

• Gantt chart - “a graphic display of schedule related information.” - PMBOK Guide.

Build the Logical Network Diagram

Enter tasks and milestones.

Understand task dependencies.

Define dependencies using a task table and mouse. 

Define or delete a dependency series.

Understand network diagram presentation.

Verify the accuracy of the network logic.

Section 7

Estimate Resource needs

• How many resources of each type and skill or knowledge level are needed.

• Consider support needs such as information systems and human resources

• Consider constraints placed upon how people are hired, scheduled and released.

• Estimate activity resources - "the process of estimating the types and quantities of resources required to perform each scheduled activity." - PMBOK Guide.

Create a staffing management plan

• Identify potential resources.

• Determine resource availability.

• Decide timing issues.

• Staffing management plan - "the document that describes when and how human resource equipment will be met" PMBOK Guide.

 Assign a resource to each activity

• Show resource responsibilities on RACI chart.

• Show resource assignments on Gantt Chart.

• Summarise resource responsibilities with histogram.

Show resource responsibilities on RACI Chart • Responsibility Assignment Matrix (RAM).

• RACI is a form of RAM.

• RACI - Responsible, Accountable, Consult, Inform.

• Responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) - "a structure that relates the project organisational breakdown to the work breakdown structure… each component of the project's scope of work is assigned to a person or team." PMBOK Guide.

A note on effort/work versus duration

• There is a difference between work and duration.

• By default, work is calculated in hours and follows this formula:

• Work = Duration * Units (W=D*U) (units refers to resources)

• Duration = Work/Units (to solve for the duration rather than work)

• Effort-driven scheduling - is when the work remains constant and the duration is changed.

◦ Work (effort) remains constant and determines (drives) the way that the W=D*U formula will be calculated.

Methods of resolving resource overloads

• Recorder the activities.

• Acquire or borrow additional resources.

• Reduce project scope or extend project schedule.

• Inform the sponsor of severe overloads.

• Resource level the overloaded person's schedule.

• Ask if the resource is willing to do overtime (with care and attention).

Resource levelling

• Delay activities so the person doesn't perform as many activities at the same time (most common).

• Delay non-critical activities by an amount no more than their slack.

• Allow the project to slip - reduces peak demand and smoothers the period to period resource usage.

• Resource levelling - "any form of schedule network analysis in which scheduling decisions… are driven by resource constraints." - PMBOK Guide.

• If non-critical activities must be completed at the rate of effort in the original schedule, reassign activities to another worker.

Compress the project schedule

• Actions to reduce the critical path.

• • Crashing.

• • Fast tracking.

Actions to reduce the critical path

• Reduce the projects scope and/or quality.

• Overlap sequential activities.

• Partially overlap sequential activities.

• Increase the number of work hours/days.

• Schedule activities at the same time.

• Shorten the duration of critical activities.

• Shorten activities by assigning more resources.

• Shorten activities that cost the least to speed up.

Compress the project schedule

 • Crashing may cost more money to speed up the schedule.

• Fast tracking may increase the risk to speed up the schedule.

• Crashing - "a specific type pf project schedule compression

 technique… performed by taking action to decrease the total project duration… how to get the maximum schedule duration for the least additional cost." PMBOK Guide.

• Fast tracking - "a specific project schedule compression technique

that change network logic to… perform schedule activities in parallel." PMBOK Guide.

Crashing

 • Certain activities are performed at a faster than normal pace.

• Crashing example - in "All-Crash" Mode.

Fast tracking

• Activities normally performed in series are performed at the same time. 

Section 8

Introduction to Project Budgeting

 • Cost management plan - "the document that sets out the format and establishes the activities and criteria for planning, structuring and controlling the project costs." PMBOK Guide.

Purposes of the Cost management plan

 • Provides feedback linking the project to business objectives.

• Provides detail and summary information.

• Helps project stakeholders focus in schedule, performance and cost.

Estimate cost

 • Cost estimating - "the process of developing an approximation of

the cost of the resources needed to complete project activities." - PMBOK Guide.

Types of costs - fixed vs variable

 • Fixed costs remain the same regardless of volume of work.

• Variable costs vary directly with the volume of use.

• Fixed and variable costs involve consideration of the project scope.

Types of costs - Direct vs indirect

• Direct costs only occur because of the project:

◦ Direct labor.

◦ Other direct costs - material, travel, consultants, subcontracts, purchased parts and computer time.

• Indirect costs are necessary costs not associated with one specific project:

◦ Buildings (eg council rates), utilities, insurance and clerical assistance.

◦ Costs are allocated across projects.

Types of costs - recurring vs nonrecurring

• Recurring costs repeat as the project work continues.

◦ Cost of writing and printing architectural diagrams; laying bricks. -Occur during project evaluation.

• Nonrecurring costs happen only once during a project.

◦ Design development.

◦ Occur during project planning and closing.

Types of costs - regular vs expedited

 • Regular costs occur when progress can be made y normal work

 hours and purchasing agreements (the preferred cost).

• Expedited costs occur when the project must be conducted faster

than normal.

-Overtime and extra charge apply.

Types of costs - estimate vs contingency

 • Estimate - "a quantified assessment of the likely amount… it should always include an indication of accuracy." PMBOK Guide.

• Reserve - "a provision in the project management plan to mitigate cost and/or schedule risk. Often used with a modifier (e.g management reserve, contingency reserve) to provide further detail on what types of risk are meant to be mitigated.”  - PMBOK Guide.

Types of costs - accrual vs cash accounting

 • Accrual - transaction are recorded in the time period the expense

 occurred.

• Cash - records transactions when the money is spent.

• Cash accounting is more frequently used on projects.

Project cost estimate comparisons

• Effort Curve: A blue line shows effort starting low during Initiating, peaking during Planning and Executing, and dropping sharply during Closing.

• Approvals: Key milestones mark each stage transition: Charter, Project Plan, Project Result, and Admin. Closure.

• Estimation Progression: As the project advances, estimates become more precise:

• Order of Magnitude: -40% to +100% accuracy (using Analogous estimating).

• Budget: -30% to +50% accuracy (using Parametric estimating).

Methods of estimating costs

• Analogous estimating.

• Parametric estimating.

• Bottom-up estimating.

Analogous estimating

 • Consider a similar project as a cost estimating starting point.

• Requires experience performing similar projects and actual cost of

 similar projects.

• Knowledge of how the proposed project differs from the previous,

• Experience with methods used to perform the project.

• Analogous estimating - "an estimating technique that uses parameters such as size, weight or complexity from a previous similar activity as the basis for estimating the same parameter or measure for a future activity." - PMBOK Guide.

Parametric estimating

 • Involves finding more information regarding the project.

• Parametric estimating - "an estimating technique that uses a statistical relationship between historical data and other variables to calculate project costs.

Bottom-up estimating

• Most detailed - specifications need to be very clear.

• Time consuming.

• Most accurate for of estimating.

• Ensure every item is included.

• Bottom-up estimating - "a method of estimating a component of work. The work is decomposed into more detail. AN estimate is prepared of what is needed to meet the requirements of each of the lower, more detailed pieces of work, and these estimates are then aggregated into a total quantity for the project." - PMBOK Guide.

Project cost estimating issues

• Supporting detail.

• Vendor and analysis.

• Value engineering.

Supporting detail

 • Describe the scope, method used to create the estimate,

assumptions, constraints and range of possible outcomes.

 Vendor Bid analysis

 • Use vendor bid analysis to determine whether the price is

 reasonable.

• For competing bids, assume the lowest responsible offer is fair.

• Prices may be determined in the market place.

Value engineering

 • Method of double-checking all the chosen methods for

 accomplishing work (cost) and the features of the project deliverables (function).

• Value is defined as the ratio of function to cost.

• A separate stage may be incorporated late in the project planning to

 ensure time is spent on value engineering.

• Value engineering - "an approach used to optimise project life

cycle costs, save time, increase profits, improve quality, expand market share, solve problems, and/or use resources more effectively." - PMBOK Guide.

Life cycle costing

 • The total costs of creating and using the project during its useful life.

• Consider disposition costs of the product after its useful life is

complete.

Time value of money

 • Discounting the value of future revenue and cost streams will enable

 better project decisions.

• Discount future dollars by the appropriate rate.

• The rate depends on the underlying inflation rate plus the cost of

capital.

Determine budget

 • Determine budget - "the process of aggregating the estimated

costs of individual activities or work packages to establish an authorised cost baseline." "PMBOK Guide.

Aggregating costs

 • Direct and indirect costs add up to the cost baseline.

• The cost baseline is an integral part of the project management

plan.

• The cost baseline can only be changed through a formal change management process.

• Cost performance baseline - "a specific version of a time-phased budget used to compare actual expenditures to planned expenditures to determine if preventive or corrective action is needed to meet the project objectives," - PMBOK Guide.
